title: 11 AI tools every product manager should learn
desc: The AI tools PMs use for research, writing, prototyping and automation, what each is best for, and the order to learn them in.
body:
AI tools now cover most of a PM's week: research, writing, design, prototyping and the repetitive work in between. You don't need all of them. You need to know which tool fits which job, and to be fluent in a few. Here's how the AI Tools Lab groups them.

Thinking and writing: Claude

Use Claude for interview synthesis, PRD drafts and critique, competitor research and data analysis. Projects keep your product context in one place, and connectors bring in Gmail, Calendar, Drive and Slack. Start here: it pays off the fastest.

Building: Claude Code, Lovable and Replit

  • Claude Code reads and edits real projects, pushes to GitHub and deploys prototypes. Best when you want full control.
  • Lovable goes from a prompt to a web app with a database, login and payments. Best for fast MVPs.
  • Replit builds and hosts full-stack apps in the browser. Good for quick internal tools.

Design: Figma and Figma Make

Design screens, build click-through prototypes and run workshops in FigJam. Figma Make generates working prototypes from a design, and Figma's MCP server lets Claude Code build from your designs.

Docs: Notion and PRD tools

Keep a product hub in Notion, write and critique PRDs with AI, and turn specs into tickets automatically.

Automation: Zapier, Make and n8n

Connect Gmail, Slack, Sheets and forms so routine work runs by itself. Zapier is the easiest to start with, Make is better for visual multi-step flows, and n8n is the most flexible and can run on your own server.

Customer-facing AI: chatbots and voice agents

WhatsApp and website chatbots answer customers with a safe handoff to people. Voice agents built on platforms like Vapi or Retell answer calls and book appointments for clinics, salons and shops.

Learn concepts, not buttons: triggers, tools, memory, evaluation and permissions last longer than any interface.

The order we recommend

Claude first, then Figma, then one builder (Lovable or Claude Code), then one automation tool. Add chatbots and voice agents when you're ready for a capstone. Every class is free in the AI Tools Lab.

title: How to become a product manager in 2026: a practical roadmap
desc: A step-by-step plan to move into product management from any background, with the skills, projects and applications that matter.
body:
Product management has no single entry path. People move into PM roles from engineering, design, sales, operations, consulting and straight out of college. What they have in common is proof that they can find a real problem, decide what to build and work with a team to ship it. This roadmap is about building that proof.

1. Understand what a PM actually does

A product manager is responsible for outcomes, not output. You decide which problems are worth solving, align engineers, designers and business teams around a plan, and measure whether the change worked. Start with Module 1 of the handbook, which covers the PM decision loop and how the role differs from project management, design and engineering.

2. Learn the core skills in order

  • Discovery: interviews, surveys and jobs-to-be-done to find problems worth solving.
  • Prioritisation: frameworks like RICE, Kano and MoSCoW, and the judgement to use them well.
  • Communication: clear PRDs, stakeholder updates and saying no with reasons.
  • Metrics: choosing a north-star metric, reading funnels and running A/B tests.
  • Tech and AI basics: enough to ask engineers the right questions and to prototype with AI tools.

3. Build three portfolio case studies

Hiring managers want to see how you think. Pick products you use and write case studies that show the whole loop: the problem, evidence, options you considered, what you chose and how you would measure success. One UX redesign, one growth or metrics case and one product strategy case is a strong mix. Our case studies show the format.

A case study with real user evidence beats ten slides of opinions.

4. Use AI tools to show you can build

In 2026, PMs who can prototype stand out. A clickable Figma flow, a Lovable app or a small automation in n8n turns your idea into something an interviewer can try. The 12-week plan walks you through one tool a week.

5. Apply with a focused story

  • Target roles where your background is an advantage, such as a fintech PM role if you've worked in banking.
  • Rewrite your resume around outcomes: what changed because of your work, with numbers.
  • Practise product sense, metrics and behavioural rounds out loud before real interviews.

Where to start this week

Read Module 1, pick the product you'll write your first case study about, and set aside five hours a week. If you'd like a plan built around your background, book a mentoring call.

title: How to write a PM case study that gets you interviews
desc: A simple structure for product case studies, the evidence hiring managers look for, and mistakes to avoid.
body:
Your case study is a sample of your thinking. Recruiters skim it in a minute, and hiring managers read it to decide whether to interview you. Both want the same thing: a clear problem, real evidence and a sensible decision.

A structure that works

  • Context: the product, the user and why this problem matters to the business.
  • Problem: one sentence, specific enough to be measurable.
  • Evidence: interviews, a short survey, reviews, screenshots of the current flow, or data.
  • Options: two or three solutions you considered, and the trade-offs between them.
  • Decision: what you'd build first and why, ideally with a prototype.
  • Metrics: the primary metric, guardrail metrics and how you'd run the test.
  • Risks and next steps: what could go wrong and what you'd learn next.

What makes it stand out

Real users. Even five short interviews make your case stronger than any framework. The Uber Find My Ride case, for example, is built on a 25-response survey and 10 rider interviews.

Show your reasoning, not just your answer.

Mistakes to avoid

  • Redesigning the whole app instead of one flow.
  • Listing features without saying which problem they solve.
  • Made-up metrics with no baseline or source.
  • Forty slides. Five to ten clear pages is enough.

Get feedback before you apply

Ask a PM to review it, or book a portfolio review. One round of feedback often turns a good case study into a great one.
